History:
• 31-year-old male presents with intensely pruritic, red, sore skin eruption.  
• Onset: 4 days ago; sudden.  
• Location: chest, hands, and flexural aspect of elbows; patient denies face, legs involvement. (Doctor later mentioned “back,” but patient never confirmed – conflict noted.)  
• Character: very itchy (“can’t sleep”), skin feels dry and “cracked”; no bleeding, pus, or vesicular discharge.  
• Aggravating/relieving: frequent warm showers give brief relief; OTC topical steroid and OTC antihistamines provided no benefit.  
• Associated symptoms: denies fever, chills, respiratory or urinary complaints.  
• Impact: interferes with sleep, concentration at work, hiking discontinued.  
• Possible triggers: none identified; no recent change in soaps, detergents, clothing reported (patient unsure).  
• Past similar episodes: prior eczema limited to arms; previous topical therapy effective at that time.

Past Medical History:
• Atopic dermatitis (eczema) – previous episode.  
• Childhood/remote asthma (resolved).  
• Allergies: NKDA (none known).  
• Medications: none on a regular basis.  – Recently used OTC topical “steroid cream” (name/dose/route/frequency not documented) and OTC antihistamines (name/dose/frequency not documented).  
• Social: lives with flat-mates; project manager in pharmaceutical company; non-smoker; drinks a few beers weekly; enjoys hiking.

Physical Examination:
• General: Appears uncomfortable secondary to pruritus; alert and oriented.  
• Skin (video): erythematous, dry, cracked patches/plaques on chest, dorsal hands, and ante-cubital fossae; no vesicles, pustules, bleeding, or exudate observed.  
• Face, legs: no visible lesions.  
• Vital signs and full systemic exam: Not recorded.

Impression:
Likely atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare.  
DDx consistent with presentation:  
1. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – acute onset; exposure history unclear.  
2. Scabies infestation – less likely; no burrows or contact history, but severe nocturnal itch raises consideration.

Management Plan:
• Prescribed higher-potency topical corticosteroid (specific product/strength not documented).  
• Prescribed emollient wash and moisturizers; instruct to apply liberally and use in bath/shower for 7–10 days.  
• Prescribed oral antihistamine (Fexofenadine; dose/frequency not documented) for pruritus; discuss trial despite limited OTC response.  
• Education: keep diary of potential triggers (soaps, detergents, clothing, environmental exposures).  
• Follow-up: re-evaluation in 1 week; sooner if worsening, spreading, or signs of infection (weeping, fever).  
• Consider dermatology referral or alternative diagnosis (e.g., contact dermatitis, scabies) if no improvement.

Patient Summary:
Four-day history of intensely pruritic, dry, cracked erythematous rash on chest, hands, and inner elbows in a 31-year-old man with prior eczema. Clinical impression is eczema flare; stronger topical steroid, emollients, and oral antihistamine initiated with close follow-up planned.

Key Takeaways:
• Apply prescription steroid thinly to affected areas twice daily (or per labeled instructions).  
• Use emollient as soap substitute and moisturizer multiple times daily.  
• Monitor rash and record any product or activity that worsens symptoms.

Next Steps:
• Return in 7 days for review or sooner if rash worsens or becomes infected.  
• If poor response, consider skin scraping for scabies, patch testing for contact allergens, or dermatology consult.

• Transcript quality: audio intermittently unclear; minor conversational gaps but clinical content largely intelligible.
